sections.title: Supplier Selection and Approval
sections.summary: Supplier selection is a structured process driven by total cost of ownership, not price alone (Deming). A cross-functional team defines criteria covering quality systems, capability, capacity, financial stability, and past performance. Suppliers are classified in tiers — Approved (meets minimums), Qualified (passed audit), Certified (consistent over time, can skip routine inspection). Industry-specific QMS standards (ISO 9001, IATF 16949, AS9100, ISO 13485) often gate approval.

concepts.definition: The process of effectively integrating and managing supply chain planning, sourcing, making, delivery, and returns of goods or services that satisfy customers' needs.
concepts.examTip: Five SCM functions: Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return. Memorize the ASQ definition verbatim.

concepts.definition: The series of processes including planning, sourcing, making, and delivering aspects of SCM — focused on ensuring inputs meet purchaser requirements.
concepts.examTip: Supplier quality is a subset of SCM, focused on the quality dimension of inputs.

concepts.definition: Process for reducing costs while improving quality, service, and innovation. Customer and supplier organizations work together for mutual benefit.
concepts.examTip: Strategic sourcing ≠ purchasing. It's collaborative and long-term, not transactional.

concepts.definition: End the practice of awarding business on the basis of price tag alone. Move toward a single supplier for any one item, on a long-term relationship of loyalty and trust.
concepts.examTip: Deming Point #4 is foundational to modern supplier management. Total cost of ownership > unit price.

concepts.definition: (1) Identify all possible sources; (2) Evaluate reputations; (3) Prepare bidders list; (4) Request bids; (5) Evaluate pre-award data; (6) Select approved supplier list; (7) Update contracts; (8) Prepare contracts.
concepts.examTip: Selection should be done by a cross-functional team (purchasing, engineering, production, quality, materials).

concepts.definition: Past performance with the product/service; sophistication of supplier's quality system (ISO 9001, IATF 16949 registration); capability to consistently meet requirements; capacity for current and forecasted demand; financial stability; technical support and partnership willingness.
concepts.examTip: Quality system, capability, capacity, financial stability, past performance — the 'big 5' selection criteria.

concepts.definition: Total cost of dealing with the supplier including material, communications, inventory requirements, and incoming verification — not just unit purchase price.
concepts.examTip: TCO = unit price + hidden costs (incoming inspection, defects, expediting, inventory carrying).

concepts.definition: Supplier meets the minimum requirements of the organization. Entry-level tier — can do business but not preferred status.
concepts.examTip: Approved is the floor; Qualified and Certified are progressively higher trust levels.

concepts.definition: Supplier has undergone additional review such as a self-assessment, questionnaire, on-site quality audit, or has obtained certificates of compliance/conformance.
concepts.examTip: Qualified = audited and passed. Higher trust than approved, lower than certified.

concepts.definition: Supplier has demonstrated consistent quality over time. May allow reduced or skip-lot incoming inspection. Eight typical criteria: timely test data, stable/in-control process, documented QMS, recent on-site QMS evaluation, recent on-site assessment, no product rejections for 1 year, no non-product rejections for 6 months, agreed-upon specifications.
concepts.examTip: Certified suppliers earn the right to bypass incoming inspection — a major cost savings for the buyer.

concepts.definition: ISO 9001 (general QMS); IATF 16949 (automotive); AS9100 (aerospace); ISO 13485 (medical devices). Often required for supplier approval in regulated industries.
concepts.examTip: Match the standard to the industry: IATF=auto, AS9100=aero, 13485=medical, 9001=general.

practiceQuestions.q: According to Deming's 14 Points, what should organizations do regarding supplier selection?
options: Award business based solely on lowest price
End the practice of awarding business on price alone
Use multiple suppliers to maximize competition
practiceQuestions.explanation: Deming's Point #4 explicitly states organizations should end the practice of awarding business on price tag alone, moving toward long-term relationships based on loyalty and trust with single suppliers.

practiceQuestions.q: A supplier who has demonstrated consistent quality over time and may receive reduced incoming inspection is classified as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A Certified supplier has shown sustained performance over time. Approved meets minimums; Qualified has passed an additional audit; Certified earns reduced or skip-lot inspection privileges.

practiceQuestions.q: Which standard governs quality management systems in the automotive industry?
practiceQuestions.explanation: IATF 16949 is the automotive-specific QMS standard. AS9100 covers aerospace; ISO 13485 covers medical devices; ISO 9001 is the general QMS standard.

practiceQuestions.q: Who should typically be involved in defining supplier selection criteria?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A cross-functional team (purchasing, engineering, production, quality, materials) defines selection criteria. Purchasing typically leads execution, but criteria definition needs broader input.

flashcards.front: What does SCM stand for and what are its 5 functions?
flashcards.back: Supply Chain Management. Functions: Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return.
End the practice of awarding business on price tag alone. Move to long-term, single-supplier relationships built on loyalty and trust.
Approved → Qualified → Certified. Approved meets minimums; Qualified passed audit; Certified has consistent track record (may skip incoming inspection).
Medical devices.
Aerospace.
Automotive.
Unit price + hidden costs (inspection, defects, inventory, expediting). Always > purchase price.

sections.title: Supplier Risk Management
sections.summary: Supplier risk management identifies, evaluates, and prioritizes supply chain risks. PMBOK defines risk as an uncertain event with positive or negative impact on scope, schedule, cost, or quality. Threat strategies: Escalate, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept. Opportunity strategies: Exploit, Enhance, Share, Accept. FMEA and fault tree analysis are primary risk assessment tools. Outsourcing transfers — but does not eliminate — risk.

concepts.definition: The identification, evaluation, and prioritization of risks to eliminate or mitigate their probability/severity, or to leverage opportunities. A risk is an uncertain event that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on project objectives (scope, schedule, cost, quality).
concepts.examTip: Risk has both negative (threat) AND positive (opportunity) dimensions — most candidates only think about threats.

concepts.definition: (1) Escalate — raise to higher authority; (2) Avoid — eliminate the threat by changing plans; (3) Transfer — shift to third party (insurance, contracts); (4) Mitigate — reduce probability or impact; (5) Accept — acknowledge without action.
concepts.examTip: Memorize: E-A-T-M-A. Escalate, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept.

concepts.definition: (1) Exploit — ensure opportunity is realized; (2) Enhance — increase probability or impact; (3) Share — partner with another party to capture; (4) Accept — take if it occurs without active pursuit.
concepts.examTip: Memorize: E-E-S-A. Exploit, Enhance, Share, Accept. Mirror of threat strategies.

concepts.definition: Systematic tool to identify potential failure modes, their effects, and prioritize them by Risk Priority Number (RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection). Used for proactive risk assessment in supplier processes.
concepts.examTip: FMEA is the most-cited supplier risk tool. RPN ranges 1–1000.

concepts.definition: Top-down deductive analysis starting with an undesired event and working backward through logical (AND/OR) gates to identify root causes and combinations.
concepts.examTip: FTA is top-down (start with failure, find causes); FMEA is bottom-up (start with components, find failures).

concepts.definition: Contracting out processes or subprocesses that don't directly contribute to core business. Reasons include lack of internal capability, cost, or strategic focus. Critical caveat: outsourcing transfers risk but does not eliminate it.
concepts.examTip: Outsourcing ≠ risk-free. The buyer retains accountability even when execution is delegated.

concepts.definition: Metrics must be meaningful, easy to understand, with low data error potential. Components should be periodically reviewed for applicability and improvement opportunities.
concepts.examTip: Bad metrics drive bad behavior — review the rating system itself, not just supplier scores.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is NOT a strategy for responding to a negative risk (threat)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exploit is an OPPORTUNITY (positive risk) strategy. Threat strategies are Escalate, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, and Accept.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the primary tool used for proactive supplier risk assessment based on Severity × Occurrence × Detection?
practiceQuestions.explanation: FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) calculates Risk Priority Number = S × O × D. FTA is also a risk tool but is top-down deductive, not numerical.

practiceQuestions.q: When an organization outsources a process to a supplier, what happens to the risk?
options: Risk is shared but accountability remains
practiceQuestions.explanation: Outsourcing transfers some execution risk but the purchaser retains accountability for outcomes. Risk is shared, not eliminated.

flashcards.back: Escalate, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept (E-A-T-M-A).
Exploit, Enhance, Share, Accept (E-E-S-A).
RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection (range 1–1000).
FTA = top-down (start with failure event). FMEA = bottom-up (start with components).
No. Outsourcing transfers execution but the buyer retains accountability.

sections.title: Supplier Communications
sections.summary: Effective supplier management requires clear, structured communication of expectations covering delivery, orders, corrective actions, safety, environmental requirements, financial expectations, and ethics. Methods range from formal written specifications, contracts, and SQA manuals to ongoing meetings, plant visits, EDI, and forecast sharing.

concepts.definition: (1) Delivery — order placement, packaging, batch sizes; (2) Order — quantity, mix; (3) Corrective action — defect response process; (4) Safety/security; (5) Environmental — pollution, hazardous substances; (6) Financial — supplier stability; (7) Management integrity & ethics — code of conduct.
concepts.examTip: Seven categories — memorize. The exam loves to ask which is/isn't a requirement category.

concepts.definition: Written specifications/drawings (hard copy or EDI); SQA (Supplier Quality Assurance) Requirements Manual; contracts and POs; terms and conditions covering IP, warranties, disclaimers.
concepts.examTip: Formal = written and binding. The SQA manual is a key supplier-facing document.

concepts.definition: Customer plant visits by technical/quality/logistics personnel; sample products provided to supplier; training delivered to supplier personnel; demand forecasts shared with suppliers.
concepts.examTip: Forecast sharing reduces bullwhip effect and supplier capacity surprises.

concepts.definition: Electronic transfer of structured business documents (POs, ASNs, invoices) between buyer and supplier systems. Reduces lead time and error rate vs paper.
concepts.examTip: EDI is fundamental to JIT and ship-to-stock programs.

concepts.definition: Supplier Quality Assurance Requirements Manual — a single document specifying QMS expectations, audit rights, performance metrics, corrective action procedures, and reporting requirements.
concepts.examTip: The SQA manual replaces fragmented requirements with one source of truth for suppliers.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven categories of requirements that must be communicated to suppliers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Marketing strategy is not a supplier communication category. The seven are: Delivery, Order, Corrective Action, Safety/Security, Environmental, Financial, and Management Integrity/Ethics.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the primary function of a Supplier Quality Assurance (SQA) Requirements Manual?
options: Provide a single source of QMS expectations and audit rights
practiceQuestions.explanation: The SQA manual consolidates QMS expectations, audit rights, performance metrics, and corrective action procedures into one supplier-facing document.

flashcards.back: Delivery, Order, Corrective Action, Safety/Security, Environmental, Financial, Management Integrity/Ethics.
Electronic Data Interchange — automated transfer of POs, ASNs, invoices between buyer and supplier systems. Critical for JIT.
Single source-of-truth document covering QMS expectations, audit rights, metrics, and corrective action procedures.

sections.title: Supplier Performance
sections.summary: Supplier performance is measured across quality, cost, delivery, and service dimensions using metrics like ppm defects, on-time delivery, Cpk, and responsiveness. Performance indices (QPI, CPI, SPI, PPI, DPI) provide composite scoring. Reports compare suppliers against best/average/worst performers and drive corrective actions, certification decisions, and business allocation.

concepts.definition: Defects (ppm); accuracy (order/billing); timeliness (on-time, JIT); completeness; responsiveness; returns for rework/repair; technical support; supplier process capability (Cpk); cost responsiveness; compliance; warranty performance.
concepts.examTip: Quality (ppm, Cpk), Delivery (on-time %), Cost (price responsiveness), Service (responsiveness) — the four main pillars.

concepts.definition: Index focused on quality dimension — defect rates, rejections. Often organized by product when no past performance history exists.
concepts.examTip: QPI = quality only. Used for new product/supplier scenarios.

concepts.definition: Tracks all materials provided by a supplier across a commodity category. Used when supplier lacks past performance history.
concepts.examTip: CPI aggregates across products in a commodity — broader than QPI.

concepts.definition: Composite index that may include quality, delivery, and best-value measures. The most general supplier scorecard.
concepts.examTip: SPI is the umbrella metric. Most scorecards roll up to an SPI score.

concepts.definition: Historical index based on quality, delivery, and other measures. Allows comparison of a supplier against its own track record or peer suppliers.
concepts.examTip: PPI = trend metric. Used for re-qualification and renewal decisions.

concepts.definition: Tracks delivery trends, scrap, supplier corrective action, and incoming inspection failures. Focused on logistics and service reliability.
concepts.examTip: DPI = delivery dimension only. On-time, in-full (OTIF) is the operational version.

concepts.definition: Statistical measure of how well a supplier's process meets specification limits, accounting for centering. Cpk ≥ 1.33 typically required for capable processes.
concepts.examTip: Cpk < 1.0 = process not capable. Cpk = 1.33 = standard requirement. Cpk = 1.67 = high-volume/safety-critical.

concepts.definition: Key questions: What is the metric's purpose? Which suppliers are critical? How much time/money will measurement require? Can the metric drive process control? What are the risks of NOT measuring?
concepts.examTip: Don't measure everything for everyone — calibrate frequency to supplier criticality and risk.

keyFigures.title: Supplier Performance Report Categories (Figure 18.1)
keyFigures.description: Standard scoring bands: Best supplier 95–100; Average 80–90 (mean ~85); Least supplier <60. Production status: Approved / Pending / Probation.

practiceQuestions.q: Which performance index would best track a supplier's delivery trends, scrap, and incoming inspection failures?
practiceQuestions.explanation: DPI (Delivery Performance Index) specifically focuses on delivery trends, scrap rates, supplier corrective actions, and incoming inspection failures.

practiceQuestions.q: A supplier's process has Cpk = 0.95. What does this indicate?
options: Process is not capable of meeting specifications
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cpk < 1.0 indicates the process is not capable. Industry standard is typically Cpk ≥ 1.33. The supplier requires improvement before approval.

practiceQuestions.q: On a typical supplier performance report, what score range represents the average of all suppliers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Average suppliers score 80–90 (mean ~85). 95–100 is best-in-class; below 60 is the worst-performing.

flashcards.back: QPI (Quality), CPI (Commodity), SPI (Supplier — composite), PPI (Past Performance — trend), DPI (Delivery).
<1.0 = not capable. 1.33 = standard. 1.67 = safety/high-volume critical.
Cpk = min[(USL−μ)/3σ, (μ−LSL)/3σ]
Quality, Cost, Delivery, Service (QCDS).

sections.title: Supplier Improvement
sections.summary: Supplier improvement combines audits (against ISO 9001, IATF 16949, AS9100, or Baldrige criteria), corrective and preventive action (CAPA), structured feedback through scorecards and meetings, and active monitoring of process improvements. Best buyers invest technical resources in their key suppliers — joint problem-solving, redesigns, and onsite support.

concepts.definition: Formal assessment of a supplier's quality system against a standard (ISO 9001, IATF 16949, AS9100) or against the buyer's own criteria. Used for qualification, surveillance, and improvement.
concepts.examTip: Audit types: First-party (self), Second-party (customer audits supplier), Third-party (independent registrar).

concepts.definition: Action taken to eliminate the root cause of an identified nonconformance. Reactive — responds to a problem that has already occurred.
concepts.examTip: Corrective = fix what already broke. Reactive.

concepts.definition: Action taken to eliminate the root causes of POTENTIAL nonconformances. Proactive — addresses risks before failure occurs. Examines the interrelationships between purchaser and supplier processes.
concepts.examTip: Preventive = stop it from breaking. Proactive. ISO 9001:2015 replaced 'preventive action' language with risk-based thinking.

concepts.definition: Eight Disciplines methodology for supplier corrective action: D1 Form team, D2 Describe problem, D3 Containment, D4 Root cause, D5 Permanent corrective action, D6 Implement & verify, D7 Prevent recurrence, D8 Recognize team.
concepts.examTip: 8D is the auto industry standard. Containment (D3) precedes root cause analysis to protect the customer.

concepts.definition: Structured periodic reports communicating supplier performance across quality, delivery, cost, and service dimensions. Reviewed in supplier business meetings.
concepts.examTip: Scorecards drive behavior — they should reinforce strategic priorities, not just measure compliance.

concepts.definition: Buyer provides technical personnel, training, or co-investment to help key suppliers solve product/process problems or jointly redesign products. Reserved for strategic suppliers where mutual benefit is high.
concepts.examTip: Joint improvement is differentiated — only worthwhile for strategic suppliers, not transactional ones.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the key difference between corrective action and preventive action?
options: Corrective fixes existing problems; preventive addresses potential problems
practiceQuestions.explanation: Corrective action responds to nonconformances that have occurred (reactive). Preventive action eliminates the root cause of potential nonconformances before they occur (proactive).

practiceQuestions.q: In the 8D corrective action process, which step comes BEFORE root cause analysis?
practiceQuestions.explanation: D3 Containment comes before D4 Root Cause Analysis. Containment protects the customer from continued exposure while root cause is being investigated.

flashcards.back: Corrective = reactive, fixes existing nonconformance. Preventive = proactive, addresses potential nonconformance.
D1 Team, D2 Problem, D3 Containment, D4 Root Cause, D5 Permanent Action, D6 Implement/Verify, D7 Prevent Recurrence, D8 Recognize Team.
First-party (internal/self), Second-party (customer audits supplier), Third-party (independent registrar like ISO).

sections.title: Supplier Certification, Partnerships, and Alliances
sections.summary: Supplier certification programs reduce incoming inspection burden — certified suppliers may be inspected only every 5th lot. Partnerships and alliances are formalized, long-term, mutually beneficial relationships. Reasons to partner: focus on core, access world-class capability, share risk, free capital, gain capacity, eliminate hard-to-manage functions. Top supplier traits: responsive/flexible service (52%), good communication (48%), high quality (29%).

concepts.definition: Allow reduced or skip-lot incoming inspection for proven suppliers. Common practice: certified suppliers receive priority for new business; only every 5th lot might be selected for incoming verification.
concepts.examTip: Certification benefit = lower incoming inspection cost + new business priority.

concepts.definition: (1) Develop certification criteria and process — identify, evaluate, select rating categories; (2) Evaluate selected suppliers against criteria; (3) Ongoing monitoring per supplier reporting requirements.
concepts.examTip: Three steps — criteria, evaluation, monitoring. Don't confuse with the 8-step selection process.

concepts.definition: Cooperative working relationship between buyer and supplier, with shared goals but typically less formalized than an alliance.
concepts.examTip: Partnership = cooperative; Alliance = formalized with shared fate.

concepts.definition: Special, formalized relationship with a supplier implying SHARED FATE, mutual benefits, and joint commitment to a common purpose. Strategic alliances are cooperative undertakings between two or more companies.
concepts.examTip: Alliance is the deepest tier — shared fate, joint investment, often equity or long-term contracts.

concepts.definition: Improve focus on core; access world-class capabilities; concentrate on strategic functions; share/reduce risk; free non-financial resources; reduce operating costs; secure unavailable resources; increase capacity; eliminate hard-to-manage functions; quickly gain new functions/services/products.
concepts.examTip: Memorize 3–4 reasons. Common exam question: 'Which is NOT a reason for partnership?'

concepts.definition: (1) Responsive and flexible service — 52%; (2) Good communications — 48%; (3) Providing high product quality — 29%.
concepts.examTip: Surprising finding — responsiveness ranks higher than quality. Service > specs in buyer perception.

concepts.definition: (1) Determine materials/services for closer relationship; (2) Address legal implications; (3) Identify candidate suppliers; (4) Define expectations and risks; (5) Communicate and negotiate; (6) Implement mutual arrangements; (7) Establish ongoing monitoring/communication.
concepts.examTip: Step 2 (legal) is critical — antitrust, IP, exclusivity issues can derail partnerships.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the primary benefit of a supplier certification program for the buyer?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Certified suppliers may receive reduced or skip-lot inspection (e.g., only every 5th lot), significantly reducing the buyer's incoming inspection cost while maintaining quality assurance.

practiceQuestions.q: What distinguishes a supplier alliance from a supplier partnership?
options: Alliances imply shared fate and formalized commitment
practiceQuestions.explanation: An alliance is the deepest tier — formalized relationship with shared fate, mutual benefits, and joint commitment to common purpose. Partnerships are cooperative but less formalized.

practiceQuestions.q: According to survey data, what is the #1 characteristic of best suppliers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Responsive and flexible service ranked #1 at 52%, followed by good communications (48%) and high product quality (29%). Buyers value responsiveness over specs.

flashcards.back: Reduced or skip-lot incoming inspection (e.g., every 5th lot only) + priority for new business.
(1) Develop criteria; (2) Evaluate suppliers; (3) Ongoing monitoring.
Partnership = cooperative. Alliance = formalized with SHARED FATE and joint commitment.
Responsive/flexible service (52%), Good communications (48%), High product quality (29%).

sections.title: Supplier Logistics and Material Acceptance
sections.summary: Logistics interfaces use push systems (forecast-driven) or pull systems (demand-triggered, including ship-to-stock). JIT extends pull principles, eliminating raw material storage by frequent small deliveries. Material acceptance options: source inspection, certification, receiving inspection, or supplier QMS history. Sampling carries Type I (producer's) and Type II (consumer's) risks. Modular assembly transfers subassembly responsibility to suppliers.

concepts.definition: Production and inventory based on forecast and demand planning. Material is pushed through the supply chain in anticipation of need. Requires close forecast/demand alignment and multi-tier schedule communication.
concepts.examTip: Push = forecast-driven, anticipatory. High inventory risk if forecast is wrong.

concepts.definition: Production and replenishment triggered by actual customer demand. Ship-to-stock is the supplier-side embodiment — material received directly without inspection, moved to point of use.
concepts.examTip: Pull = demand-driven, reactive. Lower inventory but requires reliable suppliers.

concepts.definition: Program leveraging supplier performance and certification to receive materials directly into the organization without incoming inspection. Material flows directly to point of use.
concepts.examTip: Ship-to-stock requires supplier certification first. Bypasses incoming inspection entirely.

concepts.definition: Inventory strategy where materials arrive precisely when needed for production. Reduces inventory levels and may eliminate raw material storage by frequent small-batch deliveries from suppliers.
concepts.examTip: JIT example: automotive nuts and bolts — frequent deliveries vs. large warehouse inventory.

concepts.definition: (1) Source inspection — buyer inspects at supplier site before shipment; (2) Certification — based on supplier QMS history; (3) Receiving inspection — sampling at buyer dock; (4) Supplier quality system reliance — no buyer inspection.
concepts.examTip: Risk level dictates method. Critical parts → source inspection. Certified suppliers → ship-to-stock.

concepts.definition: Risk of REJECTING a good lot during sampling inspection. The supplier (producer) bears the cost when a conforming lot is wrongly rejected.
concepts.examTip: Type I = α = Producer's risk = false rejection. Memorize: 'PR' both = Producer/Reject.

concepts.definition: Risk of ACCEPTING a defective lot during sampling inspection. The buyer (consumer) bears the cost when a nonconforming lot is wrongly accepted.
concepts.examTip: Type II = β = Consumer's risk = false acceptance. Most damaging — defective product reaches customer.

concepts.definition: Transferring additional subassembly work back to the supplier. Buyer receives a completed subassembly module, simplifying final assembly integration.
concepts.examTip: Modular assembly shifts complexity upstream. Common in automotive (e.g., complete dashboard modules).

keyFigures.title: Sampling Risks (Figure 18.2)
keyFigures.description: Type I risk (α) — producer's risk — rejecting good lots. Type II risk (β) — consumer's risk — accepting bad lots. Both risks are inherent in any sampling plan; AQL and LTPD set the boundaries.

practiceQuestions.q: Which logistics system is triggered by actual customer demand rather than forecasts?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pull system is demand-driven — production and replenishment are triggered by actual customer orders. Ship-to-stock is a pull-system implementation. Push systems are forecast-driven.

practiceQuestions.q: Type I sampling risk (α) refers to:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Type I (α) is the producer's risk — the probability of rejecting a good lot. Type II (β) is the consumer's risk — accepting a defective lot.

practiceQuestions.q: An automotive plant receives nuts and bolts in small frequent deliveries directly to the production line, with no incoming storage. This is an example of:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Just-In-Time (JIT) combined with ship-to-stock eliminates raw material storage by relying on certified suppliers and frequent small deliveries directly to point of use.

practiceQuestions.q: Which material acceptance method is most appropriate for a supplier with strong certification and consistent quality history?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Certified suppliers with strong QMS histories warrant ship-to-stock — no incoming inspection. This is the lowest-cost option and reflects earned trust.

flashcards.back: Push = forecast-driven, anticipatory, higher inventory risk. Pull = demand-triggered, reactive, requires reliable suppliers.
Receiving certified-supplier materials directly to point of use, bypassing incoming inspection.
Producer's risk — rejecting a GOOD lot. Cost falls on supplier.
Consumer's risk — accepting a BAD lot. Cost falls on buyer/end customer.
Transferring subassembly work back to supplier. Buyer receives completed module ready for final integration.
